L1879@P81: Two infantrymen wearing the service uniform in the field. This photo shows the culmination of the changes made
L1880@P81: to the Army’s uniform from 1926 to just prior to World War II including the use of the M-1917A1 Helmet, the
L1881@P81: Service Coat as a field garment, and the first pattern M-1938 dismounted leggings.
L1882@P81-82: 79Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1883@P82:  In 1940 the commander of III Corps District, Major General J. K. Parsons conducted field trials
L1884@P82: on a lightweight windbreaker type jacket meant to replace the wool service coat in the field.
L1885@P82: Specifications for the new jacket were adopted on October 7, 1940 as Jacket, Field, Olive Drab,
L1886@P82: also referred to as the “Parsons jacket.” It was made of olive drab cotton poplin with a flannel
L1887@P82: lining. There were button tabs at the waist and cuffs, and a front slide fastener closure covered
L1888@P82: by a placket secured by five brown plastic buttons. The jacket had a fall collar and notched
L1889@P82: lapels which could be closed over with a button across tab in cool weather. Finally, there was a
L1890@P82: slant pocket on each side in front, each with a flap secured by a single brown plastic button.
L1891@P82: After some further studies a second pattern was specified on May 6, 1941. The newer version
L1892@P82: had shoulder loops added and the pock flaps removed.
L1893@P82: Jacket, Field, Olive Drab, Pattern 1940 (Type I) Jacket, Field, Olive Drab. Pattern 1941 (Type II)
L1894@P82: The success of the field trial led to a change in thinking at the Quartermaster Department. The
L1895@P82: thinking now was that functional clothing should be used in the field, and separate from that
L1896@P82: worn for garrison or dress. By the
L1897@P82: beginning of 1942, the service coat was no
L1898@P82: longer seen as a field garment and was
L1899@P82: relegated to garrison and off-duty wear.
L1900@P82: It was suggested by the Office of the
L1901@P82: Quartermaster General (OQMG) that the
L1902@P82: bi-swing back could be eliminated to
L1903@P82: improve the appearance of the garment and
L1904@P82: to decrease the cost of manufacture and to
L1905@P82: save on wool. In June 1942 the "Revised
L1906@P82: Service Coat" was adopted. It no longer
L1907@P82: had the bi-swing back and the lower
L1908@P82: pockets became a simplified interior type
L1909@P82: with an exterior flap. The revised Service Coat, Pattern 1942
L1910@P82-83: 80Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1911@P83: A wide variety of specialized uniform items were introduced including clothing for parachutists,
L1912@P83: aviators, armor crewman, and so on that a beyond the scope of this study.
L1913@P83: Coat, Parachute Jumper Jacket, Flying, Cold Weather, A-2 Jacket, Combat, Winter
L1914@P83:  After extensive research and development in 1940 and 1941, the Ordnance Department in
L1915@P83: cooperation with the Infantry Board and private industry developed a new steel helmet. The
L1916@P83: body of the helmet was standardized in June 1941 as the M1. It was made from a single piece of
L1917@P83: Hadfield Manganese steel with a stainless steel rim butted and spot welded in front. Spot welded
L1918@P83: to each side was a fixed stainless steel wire chinstrap loop. The helmet was painted inside and
L1919@P83: out with an olive drab paint mixed with a cork aggregate, and two-piece khaki web chinstrap was
L1920@P83: stitch to the loops. Because the paint did not adhere well to the stainless steel rim, it was
L1921@P83: changed to Manganese in 1944, and the butt of the rim moved to the back of the helmet.
L1922@P83: The M1 helmet was designed to have a
L1923@P83: separate liner with a white rayon suspension
L1924@P83: system similar to that used in football helmets
L1925@P83: of the time. The initial liner was made of two
L1926@P83: fiber shells glued together and covered with
L1927@P83: varnished cloth. Use of the liners in the field
L1928@P83: quickly showed that they absorbed moisture
L1929@P83: and lost strength and durability.
L1930@P83: In July 1941, the Quartermaster Department
L1931@P83: began the process of finding a suitable plastic
L1932@P83: Helmet, Steel, M1
L1933@P83: liner for the M1 helmet. In February 1942, a molded, resin impregnated cloth helmet lined was
L1934@P83: adopted and contracts let for immediate production. The new liner had a suspension consisting
L1935@P83: of three loops of herringbone twill cotton tape riveted to the sides and tied together with a cord in
L1936@P83: the center. A leather and cloth headband was clipped to the suspension and could be sized
L1937@P83: adjusted with a buckle. There was also an olive drab cotton neck band that snapped into the back
L1938@P83: of the suspension, and a russet leather chinstrap that attached to an interior stud on each side
L1939@P83: towards the front.
L1940@P83-84: 81Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1941@P84: With millions of men and woman in uniform, the amount of insignia used by the Army grew
L1942@P84: dramatically, reflecting the large and complex structure of the force. Technician grades are
L1943@P84: added to the rank structure in 1942 and were reflected by a “T” centered below the chevrons. A
L1944@P84: T/5 was equal to a corporal, a T/4 to a sergeant, and a T/3 to a staff sergeant, however the ranks
L1945@P84: were not considered to be NCOs in a leadership sense. The insignia below is from a period
L1946@P84: booklet.
L1947@P84-85: 82Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1948@P85: In May 1941 it was announced that the blue denim fatigue uniform would be phased out and
L1949@P85: replaced with an olive drab, herringbone cotton twill (HBT) uniform. The new uniform was
L1950@P85: single breasted with five black metal tack buttons in front, plus a waist band with two
L1951@P85: “Burst of Glory” tack button, of
L1952@P85: three types used on the HBT
L1953@P85: uniform and other field clothing
L1954@P85: additional buttons. The jacket also had a notched lapel with a fall
L1955@P85: collar, and two patch-type breast pockets with a split pleat in the
L1956@P85: center and a flap secured by a single metal tack button.
L1957@P85: The uniform was intended for both a fatigue and field use. In
L1958@P85: November 1942, and improved version was released. Based on
L1959@P85: field experience, the breast pockets were made larger
L1960@P85: with a bellows gusset on the outer edge, and the waist band was eliminated. Treated with an
L1961@P85: anti-vesicant compound, HBTs were also used as chemical protective garments, particularly
L1962@P85: during the Invasion of France in June 1944. In March 1943, a specification change was made,
L1963@P85: changing the color of HBTs to a darker Olive Drab Shade 7.
L1964@P85: Either a hat or cap of the same olive drab herringbone twill cotton material could be worn with
L1965@P85: the HBT uniform. The hat was generally worn for fatigue while the cap was intended for wear
L1966@P85: as a work cap by mechanics and others performing similar duties, but it also became popular as a
L1967@P85: combat field cap used by troops serving in the Pacific Theater.

L1971@P85-86: 83Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1972@P86: Two soldiers of the 17th Reconnaissance Squadron awaiting transportation on New Guinea in 1944. The soldier in
L1973@P86: front is wearing a Pattern 1941 Herringbone Twill Coat. The photograph typifies the look of the combat soldier
L1974@P86: serving in the Southwest Pacific Area.
L1975@P86: In 1943 the Woman’s Army Corps joined the Army Nurse Corps as a permanent part of the
L1976@P86: Army establishment. The service and field uniforms worn by woman paralleled those worn by
L1977@P86: men.
L1978@P86:  Woman’s Summer Service Woman’s Winter Service Shirt, Herringbone Twill, Woman’s
L1979@P86:  Coat, Pattern 1942 Coat, Pattern 1942 Special, Olive Drab Shade 7
L1980@P86: In 1942 the Quartermaster Department began to look for a field uniform that could replace the
L1981@P86: variety of specialized uniforms and inadequate garments then being issued. By March 1943 the
L1982@P86: Office of the Quartermaster General recommended a uniform based on the layering principle, but
L1983@P86: had not determined the individual components of the uniform as yet. In November 1943 the new
L1984@P86: uniform was standardized as the M-1943 field ensemble. It was made of olive drab shade 7
L1985@P86-87: 84Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L1986@P87: cotton sateen and consisted of a field cap, four-pocket field jacket, detachable jacket hood, and
L1987@P87: field trousers. Liners for the jacket and trousers had been planned but were dropped in favor of
L1988@P87: the continued use of the wool service shirt and trousers. Although not strictly a part of the
L1989@P87: uniform, new combat service boots with attached leather gaiters were adopted at the same time.

L1993@P87: three members of the 92nd Infantry Division in formation
L1994@P87: wearing the Model 1943 Field Uniform and “DoubleBuckle” Combat Boots, Italy 1945.
L1995@P87: M1943 “Double-Buckle” Combat Service Boots
L1996@P87: Divisions arriving in Europe in late 1944 were
L1997@P87: equipped with this uniform as were the 82nd and
L1998@P87: 101st Airborne Divisions. Division already in
L1999@P87: Europe retained the older pattern uniform.
L2000@P87: At the same time the Quartermaster Department
L2001@P87: was developing the M-1943 uniform in cotton
L2002@P87: sateen, the high command in Europe was
L2003@P87: favoring the development of a field uniform
L2004@P87: based upon British battle dress. This uniform
L2005@P87: consisting of a waist length wool field jacket and trousers, both in olive drab shade 7, the new
L2006@P87: uniform was rarely used in the field, but by the end of 1944 it began replacing the four pocket
L2007@P87: coat and light shade trousers as the Army’s service uniform, and would come to typify the
L2008@P87: American soldier of the early 1950s.
L2009@P87-88: 85Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements

L2014@P88: Prior to World War II only marksmanship badges and service medals or ribbons were worn. As a
L2015@P88: result of the war a large variety of awards, specialty badges and qualification badges came into
L2016@P88: use.
L2017@P88-89: 86Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2018@P89: In 1948 the Army introduced a new rank structure and smaller chevrons, blue on gold for combat
L2019@P89: arms troops, gold on blue for support troops. Sergeant chevrons were eliminated and Staff
L2020@P89: Sergeants became Sergeants. In 1951 large chevrons were reinstated except for female
L2021@P89: personnel. In 1954 Specialist Badges were introduced.

L2024@P89: Corporal (Combat Arms), First Sergeant (Combat
L2025@P89: Support).

L2027@P89: Specialist - Grade 8
L2028@P89: The return to the pre-1948 chevrons as reflected in an
L2029@P89: Army manual published in 1951.
L2030@P89: In the early 1950s, the Army asked
L2031@P89: Hattie Carnegie, a popular fashion
L2032@P89: designer, to restyle the Woman’s Army
L2033@P89: Corps service uniform. The wool serge,
L2034@P89: taupe jacket she designed "had a high,
L2035@P89: round collar, slightly padded shoulders, and
L2036@P89: a nipped-in waist.” The tailoring of the
L2037@P89: matching skirt became more feminine with
L2038@P89: rounded hips and a calf length hem. The
L2039@P89: uniform was worn with a tan shirtwaist,
L2040@P89: cafe brown oxfords or pumps, and a
L2041@P89: matching service hat. Manufacture and
L2042@P89: issue of the new uniform began in 1952,
L2043@P89: and its reception by the members of the
L2044@P89: WAC was generally less than favorable.
L2045@P89: Enlisted woman also received the summer
L2046@P89: cotton dress worn with a matching garrison
L2047@P89: cap, cafe brown pumps or oxfords, tan
L2048@P89: cotton gloves, and cafe brown handbag
L2049@P89: with shoulder strap.
L2050@P89: Left, the Woman’s Taupe Service Uniform, and right
L2051@P89: the summer cotton dress both introduced in 1951.
L2052@P89-90: 87Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2053@P90: Part 2, Accoutrements
L2054@P90: Between 1919 and 1940, the Army’s accoutrements and personal equipment remained virtually
L2055@P90: unchanged. Following World War I, there were enough items on hand for every soldier of the
L2056@P90: Regular Army to be issued two sets, one for field use and one only for inspection. Items
L2057@P90: produced during World War I would continue in general use throughout World War II and, in
L2058@P90: some cases, well beyond.
L2059@P90:  (National Archives)
L2060@P90: An Army photograph of two infantry soldiers in training in 1943. The soldier on the left is wearing an M1910
L2061@P90: Haversack while the soldier on the right has a M1928 Haversack. Both soldiers have the Pattern 1917 version of the
L2062@P90: M1910 canteen and cover and, in addition the soldier on the right has an M1910 1st Aid Pouch.
L2063@P90: To be sure the Ordnance Department had made improvements to various items, but because of
L2064@P90: the quantity of items on hand and the financial situation in general, none of these items were put
L2065@P90: into production until just before the start of World War II. As a result, a number of items have
L2066@P90: model or pattern dates that are much earlier than their earliest production dates. For example, the
L2067@P90: M1923 cartridge belt, and the M1924 First Aid Pouch did not go into production until 1940.
L2068@P90: In 1936 the Army adopted a field bag (also referred to as a “musette bag”) for mounted troops
L2069@P90: and officers (later extended to airborne and mechanized personnel as well) that was a copy of the
L2070@P90: officer’s field bag used by the British Army in World War I. The old pattern equipment
L2071@P90: suspenders used by the cavalry were redesigned and D-rings were incorporated so that the field
L2072@P90: bag could be attached to the shoulder straps. The bag was designated as Bag, Canvas, Field,
L2073@P90: Olive Drab, M1936 and the suspenders were designated as Suspenders, Belt, M1936. The pistol
L2074@P90: and revolver belt was also modified enough to get the M1936 designation as well.
L2075@P90-91: 88Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2076@P91: The basic load for the infantry remained just about the same as it had been in World War I. In
L2077@P91: the early 1920s the Ordnance Department had redesigned the cartridge belt. The new belt
L2078@P91: included elements from both the pre-war belt, such as an interior strap in each pocket to assist in
L2079@P91: removing the ammunition clip, and the wartime version, such as the lift-the-dot fasteners. The
L2080@P91: result was designated as the M1923 cartridge belt.
L2081@P91: The pouch for the first aid packet was redesigned with a triangular flap secured by a single liftthe-dot fastener; the new pouch designated as the M1924. The haversack was changed by the
L2082@P91: addition of quick release buckles, and the button on the flap of the meat can pouch was replaced
L2083@P91: with a strap and buckle arrangement. It was then designated as the M1928.
L2084@P91: Between the wars, the M1910 canteen cup and cover remained unchanged, but beginning in 1942
L2085@P91: the Army experimented with making the canteen in a variety of materials including plastic,
L2086@P91: enameled steel, and corrosive resistant steel. The metal canteen cup was replaced with a black
L2087@P91: plastic cap beginning in 1942. The new cup was initially flat on top, but beginning in 1943 the
L2088@P91: cap was made with a recessed top.
L2089@P91: In 1942, the manufacture of canteen cups made of corrosive resistant steel began, although
L2090@P91: aluminum cups continued to manufacture throughout the period as well. The new steel cup had a
L2091@P91: flared edge, while the aluminum cup continued to have a rolled edge.
L2092@P91: The M1910 intrenching shovel and cover continued in use throughout the war, but beginning in
L2093@P91: 1943 a shovel with a folding blade was introduced along with a new canvas carrier. The shovel
L2094@P91: and carrier were both designated as M1943. Shortly after production of the new shovel carrier
L2095@P91: was begun, the Army changed the design by adding a gusset on the back with three pair of
L2096@P91: eyelets, one above the other. The double belt hook, instead of being in a fixed location could
L2097@P91: now be adjusted, depending on where the carrier was worn.
L2098@P91:

L2102@P91: to the belt are a Pocket, Magazine, Double-Web, Pistol, M1923, the
L2103@P91: M1910 Canteen and cover, and a Pouch, First Aid Packet, M1924.

L2113@P92-93: 90Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2114@P93: Above: The World War II version of the M1910 Infantry Equipment used with the M1 Rifle. Seen here are the
L2115@P93: M1923 Cartridge Belt, M1928 Haversack, M1943 Intrenching Tool, M1942 First Aid Pouch for the Carlisle
L2116@P93: Dressing, and the M1 Bayonet in an M7 Scabbard. Included also is the M6 Carrier for the M3-10A1-6 Light Weight
L2117@P93: Service Gas Mask; two six-pocket bandoleers to hold ammunition for either the M1 or M1903 rifle; and a view
L2118@P93: (upper right) of the M1943 Intrenching Tool and Carrier.
L2119@P93: In 1944 a new pack system was developed by the Army based upon the system then being used
L2120@P93: by the United States Marine Corps. The system consisted of three parts, the Pack, Field,
L2121@P93: Combat, M1944; the Suspenders, Pack, Field and Combat, M1944; and the Pack, Field, Cargo,
L2122@P93: M1944, that attached to the bottom of the combat pack with quick release straps. The packs
L2123@P93: were made of cotton canvas with cotton web straps; all were in olive drab shade 7. The Field,
L2124@P93: and two straps to close the main flap, two flaps with eyelets were provided: one on the top center
L2125@P93: for the intrenching tool, and one of the left side flap for the M1 bayonet. Bottom straps attached
L2126@P93: to the Cargo Pack to join the two.
L2127@P93: The suspenders could be used alone to support the weight of the pistol or cartridge belt or used to
L2128@P93: hold the combat field pack. The combat pack had a waterproof liner and interior divisions used
L2129@P93: to carry the soldiers essential items including field rations, the meat can, knife, fork and spoon, a
L2130@P93: change of underclothing and socks. A tab with eyelets at the top center of the outside of the pack
L2131@P93: was used to hold the M1943 intrenching tool and the eyelets on the left side of the flap held the
L2132@P93: scabbard for the bayonet. Spare clothing and other items not considered to be essential were
L2133@P93: packed into the cargo pack. This pack could be attached by quick released straps to the bottom
L2134@P93: of the combat pack, or if not needed, could be detached and left with the company trains. The
L2135@P93: cargo pack had a waterproof lining and web carrying handle on top so that it could be used as a
L2136@P93: furlough bag.
L2137@P93: The new pack system saw very limited field use in Europe near the end of the war, and it was
L2138@P93: soon replaced by an upgraded version designated as the M1945. The straps of the two versions
L2139@P93: were not interchangeable, so many of the M1944 pack were refitted with the new pattern straps,
L2140@P93-94: 91Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2141@P94: making the M1944 version in its original configuration, somewhat rare. The new system was
L2142@P94: adopted as Army standard and continued to be manufactured into the 1950s.
L2143@P94: 
L2144@P94: Equipment set in Olive Drab shade 7, including the M1945 Combat and Cargo Packs. Introduced near the end of
L2145@P94: World War II, this is the equipment used by the American soldier during the Korean War.
L2146@P94: Part 3, Small Arms
L2147@P94: The M1903 Rifle remained in Army service throughout the interwar years with only minor
L2148@P94: changes. Remington Arms Company began new production of the M1903 in September of 1941,
L2149@P94: at serial number 3,000,000, using old tooling from Rock Island Arsenal which had been in
L2150@P94: storage since 1919. These very early rifles are almost indistinguishable from the rifle made at
L2151@P94: Rock Island at the end of World War I. As the already worn tooling began to wear out,
L2152@P94: Remington sought approval to change and simplify the rifle speed up manufacture and improve
L2153@P94: performance. The milled parts were replaced with stamped parts and walnut stocks were
L2154@P94: replaced with less expensive but serviceable substitutes. The most noticeable visual difference
L2155@P94: was the replacement of the barrel-mounted rear sight with a smaller, simpler "peep" rear sight
L2156@P94: mounted on the rear of the receiver. The new rifle was designated the M1903A3. In early 1942
L2157@P94: the Smith-Corona Typewriter Company also began production of the M1903/A3 at its plant in
L2158@P94: Rochester, NY. Early production Remington and Smith-Corona rifles had a dark gray
L2159@P94: Parkerizing, but beginning in late 1943 a lighter gray-green finish was used. This later finish
L2160@P94: was also used on arsenal repaired weapons.
L2161@P94: The M1903 and the M1903A3 rifle were used in both training and combat during World War II
L2162@P94: and saw extensive use North Africa, Europe and in the Pacific. Ranger units in particular
L2163@P94: preferred the bolt action weapon for commando type missions.
L2164@P94-95: 92Survey of U.S. Army Uniforms, Weapons and Accoutrements
L2165@P95: M1903 Rifle with the M1905 Bayonet
L2166@P95: M1903A3 Rifle
L2167@P95: The United States Rifle, Caliber .30, M1 (also known as the Garand Rifle in honor of its designer
L2168@P95: John Garand), was the first semi-automatic rifle in the world to be generally issued to infantry.
L2169@P95: The Army began looking for a replacement for the M1903 rifle almost immediately following
L2170@P95: the end of World War I. Research and development continued at Springfield Armory into the
L2171@P95: early 1930s with numerous problems being encountered. But on November 7, 1935 a new rifle
L2172@P95: was cleared for procurement and on January 9, 1936 became Army standard as the M1 rifle.
L2173@P95: However, production difficulties and design issued continued to plague the new rifle. Finally,
L2174@P95: with the redesigned of the barrel and gas cylinder assembly in early 1940, the rifle was ready to
L2175@P95: go into full production. Output reached 600 rifles a day by January 1941, and by the end of the
L2176@P95: Army was equipped with the new rifle.
